title: By the rivers of Babylon (Psalm 136 [137])
hook: exiles weep, and the last verse is raw rage; the Church keeps it honest, not as a command

segments.voice: Yesterday, gamul, like a weaned child: a soul content to be held. Your line was quieted. Today the quiet breaks. This one is raw.

There's a reggae song with these words, and later a dance-floor hit. Bright, bouncy, easy to sing along to. The words come from a psalm, and the psalm is no party. It's exiles sitting beside foreign rivers, far from home. Their city has been burned. Their Temple is gone. And the people who carried them off stand over them and say: go on, sing us one of the songs of Sion.
screen: `A SONG FROM THE RADIO.` → `EXILES BY FOREIGN RIVERS.` → `SING US ONE OF THE SONGS OF SION.`

segments.voice: First, the history. The Babylonian army destroyed Jerusalem and its Temple, and carried many of its people away to Babylon. This psalm is their voice. In the Douay-Rheims: "Upon the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept: when we remembered Sion." They hang their instruments on the willows. Then the taunt comes, and their answer: "How shall we sing the song of the Lord in a strange land?" Second, the vow. If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, the psalmist says, let my right hand be forgotten. Jews have kept that vow close; one explanation given for the glass broken at a Jewish wedding is to remember Jerusalem even in the middle of joy. Third, the ending, and it's hard to hear. The last verse blesses whoever would take Babylon's little ones and dash them against the rock. There's no softening it. It's the voice of people who watched their own city fall. So what does the Church do with it? It doesn't pretend the verse isn't there. It keeps it in the Bible as an honest cry, not a command. The psalmist doesn't act on it; he says it to God. In the Liturgy of the Hours, the Church leaves those last verses out of common prayer. And some of the old monks read them another way: Saint Benedict, in his Rule, speaks of dashing evil thoughts against Christ, the rock, while they're still small. That's the surprise here: the Bible lets people bring even their worst anger into prayer.
screen: `THE CITY BURNED, THE PEOPLE TAKEN.` · `IF I FORGET THEE, O JERUSALEM.` · `THE LAST VERSE: RAW RAGE.` · `KEPT HONEST, NOT A COMMAND.` · then, large: `HOW SHALL WE SING THE SONG OF THE LORD?`

segments.voice: Notice one thing you're angry about, something done to you, or to someone you love, or something in the news, and name it plainly in your head without dressing it up. If you pray, hand it to God as it is, rough and unfinished, the way the psalmist did. If you don't, let yourself feel it without acting on it, and breathe out slowly.
Sion. The Douay's name for Jerusalem, remembered by exiles weeping by the rivers of Babylon, in a psalm whose last verse is rage handed over to God. Today's word.

Your line: even anger can be prayed. The week ran from a lamp to the feet, up the pilgrim road, into Jerusalem's gates, out of the depths, to a quiet lap, and now to the rivers of exile. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 136 [137] in the Liturgy of the Hours without its final verses, and read the whole psalm in scripture as the lament of the exiles.

notes: Douay-Rheims 136:1 and 136:4 given from memory; confirm.
Date of Jerusalem's destruction: 587 or 586 BC (scholars differ); the script says 587.
The Melodians' 'Rivers of Babylon' (1970) and the Boney M. cover (1978): mentioned without naming or quoting.
Liturgy of the Hours omits verses 7–9 of this psalm (per the General Instruction's policy on imprecatory verses, GILH 131); confirm the exact omitted verses.
Rule of Benedict, Prologue 28, reads Psalm 137:9 allegorically (dash thoughts against Christ); Augustine reads it similarly. Confirm.
Breaking a glass at Jewish weddings to remember Jerusalem's destruction: a common explanation among several; stated as 'at many Jewish weddings'.
